title: A first PCR over Homecoming weekend
body: Simon ran his first polymerase chain reaction this weekend. He loaded the reactions, then set the protocol on the thermocycler himself. Homecoming brings families through the building, and the lab is open when it can be. Children should see that science is a thing people do, and that the people doing it are reachable.
alt: A young boy in a lab coat and goggles setting a protocol on the thermocycler touchscreen

title: Mars analog paper accepted at Scientific Reports
body: Aalimah Akinosho, with undergraduates Nora Armstrong and Zachary Benefield, reports behavioral deficits in animals raised for six generations under Mars analog gravity and hypomagnetic fields. The paper was accepted on 23 October 2026.

title: Mackenzie Jones gives the Physiology, Neuroscience and Behavior seminar
body: Intracellular calcium kinetics in the musculature of freely moving animals: Mackenzie presented the lab's three-compartment calcium imaging in dystrophic and wild type worms to the PNB seminar series, the first student talk from the lab in the series this year.

title: Damiano Marchiafava passes his doctoral defense
body: Danny defended successfully. Hooding follows, but the defense was the event. His dissertation covers calcium handling in dystrophic muscle, including the finding that the plasma membrane calcium pump PMCA1 is downregulated before cytosolic calcium dysregulation appears.
alt: Danny at the lectern after his defense seminar, beside his closing slide

title: Invited seminar at Wayne State University
body: Andres gave the Department of Biological Sciences seminar in Detroit, titled Tracing the Origins of Dysfunction in Duchenne Muscular Dystrophy: A Multiscale Approach to Early Pathophysiology. The talk argued that the resting calcium set point is already displaced before dystrophic muscle has begun to contract, which makes the earliest pathology a problem of regulation rather than of injury. Hosted by Eleni Gourgou, with a day of meetings that included Joseph Roche, who works on Duchenne muscular dystrophy in the Physical Therapy Program there.
alt: Andres with Joseph Roche at Wayne State University, the Detroit skyline behind them

title: Naga Nidadavolu opens the fall Molecular and Cellular Biology seminar series
body: Characterization of smooth muscle pathophysiology in Duchenne muscular dystrophy: Naga gave the first MCB seminar of the semester, laying out the lab's smooth muscle program in worms and human cells, and defended her thesis proposal the same week.

title: Third R15 awarded by NIAMS
body: The National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases funded a third successive R15 for the genetic repair of muscular degeneration in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, with Xiaotian Dai as co-investigator. The lab has held continuous external funding since 2015.

title: The Big Run on Global Running Day
body: Mackenzie Jones and Andres ran Fleet Feet's Big Run 5K at Tipton Park on Global Running Day, an out and back on the Constitution Trail. Mackenzie is a marathoner as well as a master's student. The lab recommends taking the muscle out for a run now and then.
alt: Mackenzie Jones and Andres after the Big Run 5K at Tipton Park

title: Science on Tap: How animals read the Earth's magnetic field
body: A public talk for Science on Tap, given in a local pub on a Monday evening. The audience was handed paper arrows and asked to point them at their favorite holiday destination without any aids, which is the problem a migrating animal solves every year. From there: robins, spiny lobsters, hammerhead sharks and a one millimeter worm, each borrowing a different sense to read one field. Taking the work to a room where people already are is most of the point.
alt: Title slide for the Science on Tap talk, How animals read the Earth's magnetic field, with the Science on Tap Blo-No logo

title: Midwest C. elegans Meeting at the Van Andel Institute
body: A short overnight trip to Grand Rapids for the Midwest C. elegans Meeting with Mackenzie Jones and three of the undergraduate team, under the glass DNA in the Van Andel Institute atrium. Back home the same weekend, Danny and Erin represented the lab at the Phi Sigma Research Symposium and won best poster in the graduate and undergraduate categories.
alt: Five lab members standing in the Van Andel Institute atrium beneath a blue glass sculpture of a DNA double helix

title: Mackenzie Jones presents compartmental calcium analysis in Duchenne muscular dystrophy
body: Using the lab's RGBCaMP strain, Mackenzie followed calcium in the sarcoplasm, mitochondria and sarcoplasmic reticulum of freely moving animals. Dystrophic worms show higher sarcoplasmic calcium and a loss of sarcoplasmic reticulum calcium cycling. Presented at the Midwest C. elegans Meeting in Grand Rapids.
alt: Mackenzie Jones explaining her poster, Dynamic compartmental calcium analysis in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, to a visitor

title: Phi Sigma Symposium: four posters, two best-poster awards, three inductions
body: Danny, Mackenzie, Erin and Avinaash presented at the 26th Phi Sigma Research Symposium. Danny's poster on early dystrophic calcium elevation, from C. elegans embryos to human myoblasts, took best graduate poster, and Erin's on smooth muscle in Duchenne muscular dystrophy took best undergraduate poster. Erin Cheeseman, Elyssa Guleng and Nora Armstrong were inducted into the Beta Lambda chapter of Phi Sigma, the biological sciences honor society.

title: Mackenzie Jones in the Image of Research exhibition
body: Mackenzie's entry, Coloring the Secret Life of Muscles, shows calcium reporters firing along the body wall muscle of freely moving animals. The lab builds its own reporters and its own analysis, and this is what that work looks like before it becomes a figure.
alt: Mackenzie Jones beside her Image of Research entry, nine worms imaged with calcium reporters on a black field

title: Rene Wilderman presents at the University Research Symposium
body: Rene asked whether the corticosteroids given to Duchenne patients help smooth muscle the way they help striated muscle, measuring egg laying rate as the readout. The preliminary answer is that they do not, and that vamorolone, despite its reputation for reduced side effects, did not restore egg laying either. With Mackenzie Jones as second author.
alt: Rene Wilderman beside her poster on corticosteroids and smooth muscle in Duchenne muscular dystrophy

title: About half the crew in at once
body: About half of the current crew happened to be in the lab at the same time. That is rare enough to be worth a photograph.
alt: Six lab members standing together in the laboratory

title: Neuroscience and Physiology seminar at Illinois State
body: Tracing the origins of dysfunction in Duchenne muscular dystrophy, a multiscale approach to early pathophysiology. Science Laboratory Building 121, Thursday at noon.
alt: Seminar announcement for the Neuroscience and Physiology Seminar Series

title: Muscle architecture remodels during locomotion
body: Adina Fazyl and high school researcher Anbu Anbu, contributing equally, show activity dependent remodeling of muscle architecture during distinct locomotor behaviors. Accepted 16 December and live in Biology Open on 24 December, the third paper from Adina's thesis.

title: Lucas Barickman visits, eleven years on
body: Lucas worked in the lab as an undergraduate in 2015. He came back over Christmas break, now a surgeon in Switzerland, and could still pick worms with the best of them. He took the same seat at the scope and gave the camera the same look. Undergraduate research is a long game.
alt: Lucas Barickman at the bench in 2015 and back at the microscope in 2026, same pose in both

title: Adina Fazyl's image on the cover of Biophysical Journal
body: Adina's confocal image of body wall muscle was chosen for the cover of the December issue of Biophysical Journal. The same image won her an Image of Research award at Illinois State earlier in the year.
alt: Cover of Biophysical Journal showing a confocal image of C. elegans body wall muscle in yellow and magenta

title: Outstanding University Researcher Award
body: Andres received Illinois State's Outstanding University Researcher Award for 2025 to 2026, which recognizes faculty for excellence in research and requires a prior Outstanding College Research Award. The university's announcement followed in February. The award reflects the work of the students and collaborators who carried the lab through a difficult year for research funding.

title: Adina Fazyl wins the Fisher Thesis Award
body: Adina's master's thesis won the College of Arts and Sciences Fisher Thesis Award. Three manuscripts from the thesis are published, with more in preparation.

title: The Amazing World of Worms coloring book
body: A scientific coloring book for young readers, written and drawn by the lab to share what it finds interesting about a tiny nematode. Available on Amazon.
alt: Cover of The Amazing World of Worms scientific coloring book

title: Promotion to Professor
body: Andres was promoted to Professor in August 2025, ten years and eight months after the lab opened its doors.

title: Independent validation of transgenerational pathogen avoidance
body: Aalimah Akinosho and Jordan Alexander independently validated the transgenerational inheritance of learned pathogen avoidance, published in eLife. Information about a threat outliving the animal that met it is one of the three kinds of disruption the lab studies.

title: International C. elegans Meeting at UC Davis
body: The first in-person worm meeting for the lab since before the pandemic. The community gathered to celebrate Victor Ambros and Gary Ruvkun, winners of the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, and Andres roomed with Jon Pierce, his postdoctoral mentor and the person who first put a worm under his microscope.
alt: A crowded lecture hall at the International C. elegans Meeting

title: Shifat Niha and Aalimah Akinosho earn their master's degrees
body: Two graduations on one evening. Shifat worked on dystrophin isoforms in the nervous system; Aalimah on transgenerational pathogen avoidance and on life under Mars analog conditions.
alt: Two graduates in regalia holding their diploma cases at the evening commencement

title: Stretch receptors in muscle, published in Biophysical Journal
body: Adina Fazyl's paper on the mechanosensitive channel PEZO-1 in body wall muscle. Muscles express a dozen kinds of mechanical channel, and much of what they do is unresolved. Here, one of them widens the behavioral repertoire without asking the nervous system to compute anything. Accepted on the lab's tenth anniversary, 30 December 2024.
alt: Confocal image of body wall muscle fibers in yellow with magenta nuclei

title: Ten years of the Worm Lab at Illinois State
body: Ten years to the day after Andres arrived at ISU to find two new graduate students and a room full of boxes. The best part of the day is still hearing laughter from the lab all the way down the hall.

title: Adina Fazyl defends her master's thesis
body: Two years flat, with one paper published, two under review and a fourth nearing completion. Here she is taking a break to collect an award for her confocal work.

title: Jon Pierce and Koutarou Kimura visit the lab

title: The WormZapper arrives
body: Two years in the making. The instrument delivers a 1 tesla magnetic pulse in 5 milliseconds, enough to demagnetize any magnetic particle inside an animal. It is used to test magnetic orientation.
alt: The WormZapper pulse magnetizer on a bench beside an oscilloscope

title: A first paper for a high school intern
body: High school intern Adithya and graduate student Adina Fazyl published their first scientific paper, on the stretch receptor pezo-1, in microPublication Biology.

title: Celia Beron publishes in Nature

title: First human muscle cells in culture

title: Researchers to Know 2020
body: The Illinois Science and Technology Coalition named Andres among its 19 Researchers to Know for 2020, nominated by Illinois State. The entry cites the lab's work on how physical activity and intracellular calcium shape the progression of muscular dystrophy, the magnetic field work, and 130 students mentored since 2015. Credit goes to the people in the lab doing the work.

body: Published in eLife. The paper identifies a pair of sensory neurons required for the worm's orientation to the Earth's magnetic field. Students were promised donuts and coffee.

title: The burrowing behavior of C. elegans, a new assay for neuromuscular disorders
body: Accepted at Genes, Brain and Behavior. The first undergraduate paper from the group, with Celia Beron at UT Austin as first author, the first paper on C. elegans burrowing, and the lab's first work on muscular dystrophy.

title: Building a magnetic coil system from wood, wire and Legos
body: A three axis Merritt coil system with no metal in the frame, a copper mesh Faraday cage for the plates, and a tower of Legos at the center to hold the worms. With all three coils wired, the lab could neutralize and reverse every component of the Earth's field.
